Title: The efficacy and safety of electro-acupuncture for alleviating chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy in patients with coloreactal cancer: study protocol for a single-blinded, randomized sham-controlled trial.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Colorectal cancer is the most common cancer in Hong Kong. Oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy is a major first-line conventional therapy for advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer. However, oxaliplatin causes chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). Acupuncture has long been used to alleviate limb numbness in Chinese medicine. This study aims to examine the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for alleviating CIPN in patients with colorectal cancer in Hong Kong. METHODS/DESIGN: This is a single-blinded, randomized, sham-controlled efficacy trial. Eighty-four eligible patients, who are Hong Kong Chinese, aged ≥ 18 years, diagnosed with colorectal cancer and undergoing oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, will be randomized in a ratio of 1:1 to the electro-acupuncture group or the sham-controlled group. During a 12-week treatment period, patients in the electro-acupuncture group will undergo electro-acupuncture once a week from the first cycle of chemotherapy, while patients in the control group will receive sham acupuncture, and the patients in both groups will be followed up for 12 weeks. The primary outcome measure is the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy/Gynecologic Oncology Group-Neurotoxicity (FACT/GOC-Ntx) questionnaire. The secondary outcome measures include numerical rating scale (NRS) for numbness/pain, vibration and light touch sense test, the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire-C30 (EORTC QLQ-C30) and Constitution of Chinese Medicine Questionnaire (CCMQ). DISCUSSION: The study will compare electro-acupuncture with sham acupuncture to explore the feasibility for electro-acupuncture in improving symptoms caused by chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinicaltrials.gov, NCT03582423. Registered on 11 July 2018.
Abstract_Summary: This study looks at people in Hong Kong who have colon or rectal cancer and get a common chemo drug called oxaliplatin (Abstract, sentence 1)(Abstract, sentence 2). This drug can harm the nerves in the hands and feet and cause numbness and pain, called nerve side effects (Abstract, sentence 3). These side effects can make it hard for you to walk, hold things, or sleep well (Abstract, sentence 3). In Chinese medicine, we have used acupuncture for a long time to ease numb hands and feet (Abstract, sentence 4). The study wants to see if a type of acupuncture that uses a small electric current can safely help these nerve side effects in people with colon or rectal cancer (Abstract, sentence 5). The team will enroll 84 adults with this cancer who are getting oxaliplatin chemo in Hong Kong (Abstract, sentence 7). We will put people by chance into two groups: one gets real electric acupuncture once a week for 12 weeks, and the other gets a “sham” or fake acupuncture that should not have real effect (Abstract, sentence 6)(Abstract, sentence 8). We will use simple question forms and touch tests to see if numbness, pain, and daily life get better (Abstract, sentence 9)(Abstract, sentence 10). The study will show if this kind of acupuncture is a useful and workable way to ease chemo nerve side effects (Abstract, sentence 11).
Full_Text_Summary_With_In_Text_Citations: This study looks at people in Hong Kong who have bowel cancer and get a drug called oxaliplatin, which often causes nerve pain and numb hands and feet called chemotherapy‑induced peripheral neuropathy, or CIPN (Abstract, para. 1). We need this study because many people on this drug, up to almost all of them, get these nerve side effects, and there is no clear, proven way to ease them yet (Introduction, para. 1)(Introduction, para. 2). If you have bowel cancer and feel tingling, pain, or numbness in your hands or feet during treatment, this research may help you in the future (Abstract, para. 1). The team will sign up 84 adults with stage II–IV bowel cancer who are starting oxaliplatin and do not already have nerve damage (Methods, para. 1)(Methods, para. 2)(Methods, para. 3). They will split people by chance into two groups: one gets real electro‑acupuncture once a week for 12 weeks, and the other gets a “sham” treatment where needles touch but do not go into the skin (Abstract, para. 2)(Methods, para. 18). They will use a symptom survey and simple pain and touch tests over about 24 weeks to see if real acupuncture works better than sham (Abstract, para. 2)(Methods, para. 19)(Methods, para. 20). If this trial shows that acupuncture is safe and helps CIPN, doctors could plan larger studies and may later use it as an add‑on care choice for people on this type of chemo (Abstract, para. 3)(Discussion, para. 2)(Discussion, para. 4).
